newsitem.title: USA: CSX sees Conrail deal OK in early 1998.
newsitem.headline: CSX sees Conrail deal OK in early 1998.

text.p: CSX Corp said it expects the federal Surface Transportation Board to approve the proposed purchase of Conrail Inc in early 1998, paving the way for substantial savings and earnings growth.

In a conference call with Wall Street analysts, CSX chief financial officer Paul Goodwin said the railroad expects to achieve $75 million of synergies in the first year of the transaction, $170 million in the second year and $240 million in the third year.
Two-thirds of those synergies are expected to come from cost reductions, he said.
Other benefits are expected from capital expenditures savings, which should begin at $12 million in 1998 and build to $40 million by the third year of the deal, he said.

CSX and Norfolk Southern Corp late Tuesday detailed the division of assets from Conrail. The proposed $10.3 billion deal calls for Norfolk Southern to pay $5.9 billion for 58 percent of Conrail and CSX to pay $4.3 billion for 42 percent of the East Coast railroad.
CSX plans to finance the deal by raising $2.0 to $2.5 billion in capital markets, prompting debt levels to peak at $6.4 billion in 1998, Goodwin said.

Goodwin said the acquisition is expected to dilute earnings per share by one percent in 1997, have a break-even impact in 1998 and be accretive to earnings by eight percent in 1999 and 12 percent in 2000.
CSX anticipates booking $80 million in goodwill for the Conrail acquisition, Goodwin said.
CSX chief executive officer John Snow praised the outcome of the five-month battle for control of Conrail.
"It results in nothing less than a powerhouse company. We're getting the parts of Conrail that fit best with us," he said, adding that the CSX system can absorb the Conrail assets with relative ease.
